 7   Q.    PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME, TITLE, AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 8   A.    My name is Scott Norwood. I am President of Norwood Energy Consulting, L.L.C. My

 9         business address is 5926 Lookout Mountain Drive, Austin, Texas 78731.

10

11   Q.    WHAT IS YOUR OCCUPATION?

12   A.    I am an energy consultant specializing in the areas of electric utility regulatory consulting,

13         resource planning and energy procurement.

14

15   Q.    PLEASE       SUMMARIZE             YOUR    EDUCATIONAL            BACKGROUND            AND

16         PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE.

17   A.    I have 45 years of experience in the electric utility industry. After graduating from the

18         University of Texas in 1980 with a Bachelor of Science degree in electrical engineering, I

19         began my career as a power plant engineer for the City of Austin’s Electric Utility

20         Department where I was responsible for electrical maintenance and design projects for the

21         City’s three gas-fired power plants. In January 1984, I joined the staff of the Public Utility

22         Commission of Texas (“PUCT” or “Commission”) as Manager of Power Plant

23         Engineering. In that capacity, I was responsible for addressing resource planning, fuel and

24         purchased power cost issues presented in regulatory filings before the Texas Commission.

25         In 1986, I joined GDS Associates, Inc., a Marietta, Georgia-based consulting firm that

26         specializes in electric utility regulatory consulting and resource planning. I was elected a

 2         January 2004, when I left GDS to form Norwood Energy Consulting, LLC. The focus of

 3         my current consulting practice is electric utility regulatory consulting. Exhibit SN-1

 6   Q.    ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU TESTIFYING IN THIS CASE?

 7   A.    I am testifying on behalf of the City of El Paso (“City”).

 8

19         fuel, and power plant certification matters before state regulatory commissions in Texas

20         and 15 other states, including Alaska, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Iowa, Michigan,

21         Missouri, New Jersey, Louisiana, Ohio, Oklahoma, Virginia, Washington, and Wisconsin.

  1   Q.       WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY?

 2   A.       The purpose of my testimony is to present my findings and recommendations regarding

 3            EPE’s application for approval of a new High Load Factor Large Power Service

 4            (“HLFLP”) tariff for service to Wurldwide LLC, a new large data center customer, and

 5            other large high load factor customers.

 6

 7   Q.       HAVE YOU PREPARED ANY EXHIBITS TO SUPPORT YOUR TESTIMONY?

 8   A.       Yes. I have prepared 12 exhibits, which are attached to my testimony.

 9

10                                       II.      SUMMARY OF TESTIMONY

11   Q.       PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR TESTIMONY AND RECOMMENDATIONS.

12   A.       My primary conclusions and recommendations regarding EPE’s proposed HLFLP tariff

13            are as follows:

14                     1)    EPE’s HLFLP tariff application does not address the rate impacts to existing

15            customers1 of service that it proposes to provide under the HLFLP tariff.                   In fact, EPE

16            admits that it has not evaluated incremental costs or rate impacts of service that would be

17            provided to data centers and other large high load factor customers under the HLFLP tariff.2

18            Without such information, there simply is no basis for concluding that the HLFLP tariff

19            will provide service at rates that are just and reasonable, and not unreasonably preferential

20            or discriminatory.

 4           all costs necessary to obtain electric service and shall not adversely impact charges to

 6                    3)   EPE has also not conducted analysis of the incremental cost and rate impacts

 7           of the option for the large high load factor customers who take service under the HLFLP

 3           factor customers such as Wurldwide who require tariff terms and conditions and

 4           contractual commitments that are not typically required by large customers.6

 5

 6   Q.      WHAT IS THE BASIS FOR RATES PROPOSED UNDER EPE’S HLFLP TARIFF?

 7   A.      EPE asserts that the rates offered under the HLFLP tariff are “cost-based” charges that

 8           were initially approved under its existing Rate Schedule 33A, which is an economic

 9           development rate originally approved by the Commission in Docket No. 56903 for service

10           to Wurldwide.7        The Company requests approval to terminate Rate Schedule 33A and

11           replace it with new Rate Schedule 27, the HLFLP tariff. 8

15           Contract Demands equal to or higher than 75 MW and with expected annual Load Factors

16           equal to or higher than 85%.9

 8   Q.        IS THIS THE APPROPRIATE PROCEEDING FOR THE RELIEF SOUGHT BY

 9             EPE OR SHOULD THE COMMISSION REQUIRE THE COMPANY TO

10             REQUEST APPROVAL OF THE HLFLP TARIFF IN A BASE RATE

11             PROCEEDING OR OTHER PROCEEDING? (PRELIMINARY ISSUE NO. 1)

12   A.        No. This is not the appropriate proceeding for approval of EPE’s proposed HLFLP tariff

13             because the Company has not demonstrated that the tariff is just and reasonable and that it

14             would not result in adverse rate impacts to existing customers or that existing customers

15             subsidize the incremental cost of serving data centers or other large high load factor

16             customers.11 For this reason, it would be appropriate to delay the final approval of the

17             HLFLP tariff until a future base rate case or other proceeding, so that EPE can analyze and

18             present the incremental cost of service and rate impacts of the proposed tariff and

19             demonstrate that existing customers would not subsidize service provided to data centers

20             and other large customers under the tariff.

21

  1   Q.       HAS EPE DEMONSTRATED THAT THE PROPOSED HLFLP RATES ARE JUST

 2            AND REASONABLE, NON-DISCRIMINATORY, SUFFICIENT, EQUITABLE,

 3            AND CONSISTENT IN APPLICATION TO EACH CUSTOMER CLASS?

 4            (PRELIMINARY ISSUE NO. 4)?

 5   A.       No. Again, EPE has simply not conducted the analysis required to determine whether the

 6            proposed HLFLP rates are just and reasonable, non-discriminatory or equitable to each

 7            customer class. Even when those updated rates are approved, they will reflect only an

 8            update of the Schedule 33A rates to the cost of service approved in Docket No. 57568, not

 9            any analysis of the incremental cost of servicing customers under the HLFLP tariff, and

10            the Docket No. 56903 Stipulation provides for the rates to be updated in this manner only

11            until the customer is included in a full rate case.12 In addition, EPE has not evaluated the

12            potential impacts of the option for customers who take service under the HLFLP tariff to

13            serve a portion of their contract demand and energy usage from renewable energy resources

14            under the Company’s GEP tariff.13 The lack of analysis of the cost and rate impacts of

15            customers who take service under the HLFLP also taking service under the GEP tariff

16            creates additional uncertainty as to ultimate cost impact of the HLFLP tariff on EPE’s

17            existing customers.        This is because by taking service under the GEP tariff, large high

18            load factor customers could avoid a portion of the high incremental cost of capacity

19            acquired by EPE to serve such customers.

 3   A.       The proposed 20-year minimum initial term for service under the HLFLP, which includes

 4            a maximum 4-year ramp period14 reasonably compares to the minimum terms of service

 5            large high load factor customer tariffs of other utilities in Texas and other jurisdictions that

 6            I have reviewed.15 For example, Southwestern Electric Power Company (“SWEPCO”)

 7            recently agreed to a large high load factor customer tariff with a 18-year minimum initial

 8            term as a provision of a Unanimous Stipulation and Settlement Agreement filed in PUC

 9            Docket No. 58796.16 In addition, Southwestern Public Service Company (“SPS”) has a

10            pending application in PUC Docket No. 60332 for approval of a large load tariff that

11            proposes a minimum 15-year initial term including a maximum 5-year ramp period.17

12                     However, the extent to which EPE’s proposed 20-year minimum term is

13            appropriate to protect the Company and its existing customers from potential stranded costs

14            incurred to serve large high load factor customers also depends in large part on the types

15            of new resources that are acquired to serve large customers, as well as other factors such

16            as the minimum billing demands and security provisions of tariff. For example, if EPE

17            acquires a new gas-fired combustion turbine (“CT”) unit, which typically would be

18            expected to have a service life of 40 years or more, the 20-year minimum term under the

19            HLFLP tariff would not fully insulate existing customers from the potential stranded cost

20            that remains after the initial term of service to Wurldwide expires. Unfortunately, EPE

 6   Q.       WHAT TARIFF PROVISIONS ARE SUBJECT TO MODIFICATION BY

 7            MUTUAL AGREEMENT OF EPE AND A CUSTOMER TAKING SERVICE

 8            UNDER THE PROPOSED HLFLP TARIFF? (PRELIMINARY ISSUE NO. 6)

 9   A.       The HLFLP tariff appears to provide significant leeway for the Company and a large

10            customer to negotiate terms and pricing of service under the ESA and thereby diminish

11            customer protections provided under the HLFLP tariff.                  For example, the tariff requires

12            that the load ramp period no exceed four year or for such period as allowed by the

13            Company, it leaves to the ESA which components of the Demand Charge are subject to the

14            85% minimum billing demand, it provides that the amount and duration of the Facility

15            Charge shall be determined by a separate agreement, it provides that the Company and the

16            customer will agree on an Initial Security Amount, and the ESA form includes a blank

17            Section 10 for Additional Terms.19 Each of these is a point at which the protections of the

18            tariff could be negotiated away without Commission review. I therefore recommend that

19            the Commission make clear that no ESA term may be less protective of existing customers

20            than the tariff itself.

 8   Q.        WHY IS IT IMPORTANT FOR FINAL APPROVAL OF THE HLFLP TARIFF TO

 9             BE DEFERRED UNTIL A FUTURE PROCEEDING?

10   A.        EPE has not yet conducted the incremental cost and rate impact analyses needed to

11             demonstrate that the HLFLP would not adversely impact the Company’s existing

12             customers. This analysis is essential considering the fact that the Company indicates that

13             it expects to serve between 1 and 2 GW of new load under the HLFLP over the next 3

14             years.22 Until EPE has fully evaluated the cost and reliability impacts of serving this

15             enormous load growth it would simply not be prudent to march forward with offering

16             service under terms of the proposed HLFLP tariff, unless approval is conditioned on EPE

17             holding its existing customers harmless from the incremental costs of that service, as I

18             recommend above.

  1   Q.        ARE YOU AWARE OF OTHER UTILITIES THAT HAVE OFFERED A HOLD

 2             HARMLESS GUARANTEE TO PROTECT EXISTING CUSTOMERS FROM

 3             POTENTIAL ADVERSE IMPACTS OF SERVICE PROVIDED TO LARGE HIGH

 4             LOAD FACTOR CUSTOMERS?

 5   A.        Yes. Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company (“OG&E”) recently proposed a customer hold

 6             harmless provision in conjunction with a pending application for approval of a large load

 7             high load factor tariff.23 Moreover, the Trump Administration’s Ratepayer Protection
